solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Top Europeans dismissing article essentially blaming economic system (10)

indicators.note: ITALIANS sends away the article AN
the essence of a word is its middle letter

blocks.note: a cap tops the head
ITALIANS without AN, the indefinite article
the middle letter of the seven in BLAMING

explanation.surface: A grumble that the leading nations of Europe are pinning the blame on the economic system.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface splits at 'Top Europeans', but 'Top' is a separate piece (CAP) and 'Europeans' loses AN on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Capitalism is the economic system built on private ownership and markets.

clue.text: New revolutionary regularly annoys older national hero (6)

indicators.note: a revolution turns something round, so the letters run backwards
something done regularly happens at even intervals, so only every second letter is kept

blocks.note: N = new
the even letters of aNnOyS oLdEr, NOSLE, turned round

explanation.surface: A young firebrand keeps needling an older figure who is a national hero.
explanation.walkthrough: The alternate letters run across two words, 'annoys older', and are then read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the admiral who won Trafalgar is Britain's classic national hero.

clue.text: Bacon, perhaps? It’s easy to cook small cuts (8)

indicators.note: cooking the letters mixes them up
S cuts into the mixed letters, landing inside them

blocks.note: ITS EASY rearranged
S = small, cut into ESAYIST after its first two letters

explanation.surface: A kitchen tip: bacon is easy to cook if you use small cuts.
explanation.walkthrough: Bacon is the Elizabethan writer Francis Bacon, famous for his Essays, not the rasher the kitchen surface suggests; 'perhaps' flags him as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Bacon wrote the Essays, so he is an example of an essayist.

clue.text: French craft utilising different topping for cake (6)

indicators.note: the first letter, the top of a down entry, is swapped for another

blocks.note: bateau is French for boat; its top letter B goes
a new top letter replaces the B

explanation.surface: A French boat fitted with a new top, perhaps for a fancy cake decoration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topping' sounds like icing, but here it means the top letter of this down answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A borrowed French word for a rich cream cake, so a plain synonym with a French accent.

clue.text: Endless craze strangely to purchase former PM’s sideboard (8)

indicators.note: CRAZE loses its last letter
the remaining letters are arranged strangely
to purchase is to take in, so the letters take in EDEN

blocks.note: CRAZ(e) rearranged, split CR…ZA
Anthony Eden, Prime Minister 1955–57, goes inside

explanation.surface: A strange fad has people buying the sideboard that once belonged to a former Prime Minister.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthony Eden was a British Prime Minister in the 1950s, a favourite crossword EDEN.
explanation.definitionFit: A credenza is a sideboard or low cabinet for serving or storage.

clue.text: Hang vertically we hear to obtain fruit (4)

indicators.note: the answer is what we hear, not what is written

blocks.note: to plumb is to hang straight down, like a plumb line

explanation.surface: An instruction to let something hang straight down to reach the fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: PLUMB and PLUM sound the same; the silent B drops out.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the purple stone fruit is one kind of fruit among many, so the clue names only the class.

clue.text: Oscar-winning film produced, inspired by two Americans (7)

indicators.note: breathed in by the two Americans, so it goes inside them

blocks.note: A and US, two ways to say American
made = produced, placed between A and US

explanation.surface: A note that an Oscar-winning film was made with two Americans as its inspiration.
explanation.walkthrough: The two Americans are different: A is an abbreviation for American and US is the country.
explanation.definitionFit: Amadeus, Milos Forman's 1984 film about Mozart, won Best Picture.

clue.text: Oliver in fact trained under adult in plant (7,6)

indicators.note: the letters are trained into a new shape
in a down answer, what comes under follows

blocks.note: A = adult, as in film ratings
OLIVER IN FACT rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone called Oliver actually trained under a grown-up at a factory plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plant' reads as a factory in the surface; it is the houseplant.
explanation.definitionFit: The African violet is a popular flowering houseplant.

clue.text: Paint a circle almost, roughly surrounding yard (7)

indicators.note: CIRCLE is not quite complete, losing its last letter
done roughly, the letters come out jumbled
the jumbled letters go around Y

blocks.note: A as written
CIRCL(e) rearranged, split CR…LIC
Y = yard, placed inside

explanation.surface: Painting a circle, only roughly, around a yard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roughly' tempts as C for circa, but here it jumbles CIRCL.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the quick-drying plastic-based medium is one kind of artist's paint.

clue.text: Prime ministers, maybe those regularly using planes? (13)

blocks.note: prime ministers choose, and so make, their cabinets
furniture makers use carpenters' planes all the time

explanation.surface: A question whether prime ministers are the people always flying about in planes.
explanation.walkthrough: The planes are woodworking tools, not aircraft, and the first sense is a pun: a prime minister makes a Cabinet by appointing it.
explanation.definitionFit: Cabinet-makers build fine furniture; prime ministers make up their cabinets of ministers.

clue.text: Restore government control at first (9)

indicators.note: control comes first, before government

blocks.note: to rein in = to control
the state = the government

explanation.surface: A demand to bring back government control in the first place.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces appear in the clue in the wrong order, and 'at first' tells you to put control before government.
explanation.definitionFit: To reinstate is to restore someone or something to a former position.

clue.text: Type of happy person this writer visits when upset (5)

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside someone's home, so ME goes inside the person
upset means turned over, so once ME is inside, the whole thing runs backwards

blocks.note: a bod is a person
the setter, referring to themself

explanation.surface: The setter drops in on a cheerful person who has had a bad time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Demob happy' describes the giddiness of someone about to be released from duty; the answer completes that phrase. A 'bod' is British slang for a person.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: British 'demob happy' is the elation of soldiers about to be demobilised, so the answer is the word that types that happiness.

clue.text: Comedian has no place making series (5)

indicators.note: the comedian's name is left without PL

blocks.note: Charlie Chaplin, the silent-film comedian
PL = place, as in street addresses; removed

explanation.surface: A comedian without a venue to play is unable to put on a series.
explanation.walkthrough: PL is the abbreviation for Place in addresses.
explanation.definitionFit: A chain is a series of connected things, like a chain of events.

clue.text: Dinosaur bone discovered by retired academic early in August (9)

indicators.note: BONE uncovered loses its outer letters
ON sits beside the other part
retiring means going back, so the letters reverse

blocks.note: DON (a university teacher) and AUG I (the first of August), read backwards
(b)ON(e) with its covering letters taken off

explanation.surface: A dinosaur bone turned up by a retired professor at the start of August.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Early in August' is a date, 1 Aug, written AUG I in Roman numerals, and it reverses along with DON.
explanation.definitionFit: Iguanodon was a large plant-eating dinosaur, one of the first identified from fossil bones.

clue.text: Australian music producer made love, embracing Spice Girl before party (10)

indicators.note: DID…O holds the next part inside
before means in front of, so the Spice Girl is placed ahead of the party

blocks.note: did = made, as in 'did a cake'
Geri Halliwell of the Spice Girls
a do is a party
O = love, zero in tennis

explanation.surface: Someone made love to a Spice Girl before a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made love' looks like one phrase but splits into DID and O. The music producer is an instrument, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: The didgeridoo is the long wooden drone instrument of Aboriginal Australia, which produces music.

clue.text: Wearing a singlet, one appearing later most childlike (7)

indicators.note: the I moves further along the string

blocks.note: IN = wearing, as in 'in a hat'; its I is the one that moves
A as written
I = one, the I of IN turning up after A
a singlet is a vest

explanation.surface: Someone in a singlet turning up late comes across as the most childish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wearing a singlet' builds IN A VEST, then its I jumps from the front to sit after the A. A singlet is a vest in Britain, a sleeveless undershirt.
explanation.definitionFit: Naive means innocent as a child, so the superlative is the most childlike.

clue.text: Son stops old singer developing muscle (8)

indicators.note: S stops up the singer, plugging the gap inside

blocks.note: ex = former
a tenor sings
S = son, placed inside TENOR

explanation.surface: A son takes over from an old singer who is building up a muscle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Developing' links the wordplay to the definition: the pieces develop into a muscle.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: this is the kind of muscle that extends, or straightens, a limb.

clue.text: Praise parking large car close to juggernaut (7)

blocks.note: P = parking, as on road signs
L = large, as on clothes labels
the German car make
the last letter of JUGGERNAUT

indicators.note: the close of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: Credit for parking a big car right up against a lorry.
explanation.walkthrough: A juggernaut is British slang for a very large lorry; only its last letter is used.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from the Latin for 'applaud!': it is a formal word for praise.

clue.text: Loud item of jewellery (8)

blocks.note: used of a sound so shrill it seems to stab the ear
a stud or ring worn through the skin

explanation.surface: A description of a flashy piece of jewellery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loud' reads as garish jewellery, but it is a separate definition about sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A piercing noise is loud, and a piercing is a piece of body jewellery.

clue.text: Conference backs banning outsiders? Suggest it’s permanent (9)

indicators.note: the conference goes backwards
the outer letters are removed

blocks.note: SUMMIT, a top-level conference, reversed to TIMMUS without its outer T and S
to table a proposal is to put it forward

explanation.surface: A conference supports excluding outsiders, and someone proposes making that permanent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backs' reads as supports but tells you to reverse SUMMIT. In Britain, to table a motion is to propose it.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: what cannot be changed, from Latin mutare, to change, is permanent.

clue.text: Robbed of hat touring France … (6)

indicators.note: the hat goes all round France

blocks.note: a flat round cap
F is the international vehicle code for France, placed inside

explanation.surface: A beret stolen while touring France, running on into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis joins this surface to 20 down, but the two clues are solved separately.
explanation.definitionFit: Bereft of means deprived of, just as robbed of does.

clue.text: Content to share national sporting venue (5)

indicators.note: the answer is the content held inside the next words

blocks.note: the letters run from the third of SHARE into the start of NATIONAL

explanation.surface: Being happy to share the national sports ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Content' reads as happy, but it means contents, what the words hold: sh(ARE NA)tional.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: from the Latin for sand, the sanded floor of a Roman amphitheatre, now any enclosed ground for sport.

clue.text: … risks wasting day in French city (6)

indicators.note: the day is wasted, thrown away

blocks.note: dangers = risks
D = day, removed

explanation.surface: Running on from 19 down: the risks of losing a day in a French city.
explanation.walkthrough: ANGERS looks like the English word for rages, but it is a city on the Loire.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the old capital of Anjou, on the Loire, is one French city.

clue.text: Someone unattractive and extremely detestable sacked by French newspaper (5)

indicators.note: take the extremes, the first and last letters
those letters are fired from the newspaper name

blocks.note: Le Monde, the Paris daily
the outer letters of DETESTABLE, removed

explanation.surface: An ugly, hateful man gets fired by a French newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang a lemon can be a dull or unattractive person.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional use: in British slang the sour fruit names a plain, unappealing person.

clue.text: Māori tattoo is instant hit (4)

blocks.note: a mo is a moment, as in 'half a mo'
KO = knockout, a knockout blow

explanation.surface: A claim that the Māori tattoo became an overnight success.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Instant hit' reads as a runaway success but splits in two. 'Half a mo' is British for a moment.
explanation.definitionFit: Moko is the traditional Māori tattoo of the face and body.

clue.text: Identify England’s opener after scoring runs taking drug (9)

indicators.note: the first letter of England
after means following, so England's E is placed behind the jumbled letters
SCORING runs into a new order
the jumbled letters take the drug in with them

blocks.note: SCORING plus E (ecstasy) rearranged
the first letter of ENGLAND, placed after

explanation.surface: A cricket scandal: England's opening batsman, after scoring runs, is caught taking drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket surface makes 'runs' look like the score, but it tells you to mix up SCORING with E, the usual abbreviation for ecstasy.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to know someone again on sight is to identify them.

clue.text: Become popular and successful in skit (4-3)

blocks.note: like a plane leaving the runway, a product can suddenly soar
a comic impression mimicking someone

explanation.surface: An actor makes their name through a comic sketch.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb phrase and the hyphenated noun share letters; the enumeration (4-3) follows the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom for sudden success, like a plane climbing, and a noun for a comic impression that mimics someone.

clue.text: Channel keen ultimately to have darts (7)

indicators.note: the ultimate, last, letter of KEEN

blocks.note: the last letter of KEEN
arrows is slang for darts in the pub game

explanation.surface: A TV channel eager to show darts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Channel' reads as a TV station but is a narrow stretch of water. In British pubs darts players call their darts arrows.
explanation.definitionFit: The narrows is a narrow channel of water between two larger bodies.
